items.summary:

How AI is helping scientists uncover new leads for understanding and treating neurodegenerative diseases—and the brain research behind our collaboration with @perturbai_tx and @scrippsresearch:


Video
OpenAI (@OpenAI)

GPT-Rosalind surfaced a new lead for drug discovery: could restoring cholesterol transport protect neurons from degeneration?

DCTN1 is a gene linked to Perry syndrome, a rare neurodegenerative disorder. In mouse-brain data, disrupting it increased expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. GPT-Rosalind suggested a possible explanation: cholesterol may not be reaching where neurons need it.

That gives scientists a specific mechanism to test and, if confirmed, a direction for developing new treatments for neurodegenerative disorders.

With @perturbai_tx and @scrippsresearch, a team of thousands of GPT-Rosalind agents worked in parallel, connecting gene-expression results from millions of mouse brain cells with scientific literature in just 32 minutes. We’re now expanding this collaboration to identify new drug targets.

items.title: @AIatMeta
items.summary:
·

muse ember, fast, cheap, and plenty performant

Justin Lo (@loresjpg)

So, we tested Qwen 4 Max on MaxxBench. Yeah... you should probably just use DeepSeek for coding.

In other news, Muse Ember is actually stupidly fast, really cheap, and pretty good! If you're going to use DeepSeek, you should probably just use Muse Ember.

— https://nitter.kareem.one/loresjpg/status/2123828478764368033#m
·

We recently brought together researchers from across academia, national labs, healthcare, and policy for the Open Source AI for Science Summit to explore how open models from Meta, such as Muse Glimmer, SAM, DINO v3, TRIBE v2 and UMA, are driving real-world advancements.

A couple highlights:

→ Medical Research: The University of Pittsburgh presented an assistive-robotics system built on DINOv3 and SAM 3. The team plans to demonstrate a robot that can help a person eat and is experimenting with letting users give instructions in their own words.

→ Chemistry: With the University of Chicago, we showed how UMA can simulate entire enzymes, atom by atom, potentially helping scientists understand how they work and engineer better ones for medicine, sustainability and energy.

Read the full recap: go.meta.me/4Cg6mBI
